title: Intel CEO Hints Chipzilla’s Return To Making Memory, As He Teases “New Memory Architecture” & 3D Stacking To Tackle The DRAM Wall
gist: On the TechSurge Deep Tech VC Podcast, Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan reversed his long-held view that memory is a commodity and hinted at an Intel return to DRAM via new architectures, CPU-plus-stacked-DRAM designs, and the in-progress XBM and ZAM projects timed for 2029-2030 — reinforced by hiring ex-SK Hynix CEO Seok-Hee Lee to run foundry and advanced packaging.

insights.claim: Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan says he personally avoided investing in memory because it was a commodity business, but that AI-driven market dynamics have changed enough that he no longer views it that way.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: A capital allocator publicly de-commoditizing memory is a regime-change marker for memory multiples — it argues the cycle's trough valuations no longer apply.
insights.quote: I used to be don't invest in memory because it's kind of commodity business right but now become different there's a lot of new technology come out so we are kind of looking at.
insights.locator: I used to be don't invest in memory

insights.claim: Tan describes a new memory architecture as one of his personal pet projects at Intel and says the company is not ready to unfold it yet, signalling an undisclosed program rather than a formal roadmap item.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Treat any Intel memory announcement as an option, not a plan — but one with CEO-level sponsorship, which raises the odds it gets funded through downturns.
insights.quote: One of my pet project is looking some of the memory new architecture

insights.claim: Intel's hire of former SK Hynix CEO Seok-Hee Lee as EVP of the foundry business and advanced packaging technologies is presented as the clearest tell of the company's memory intentions.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Executive hires from memory incumbents are a cheap early read on strategy shifts; watch for further SK Hynix/Samsung DRAM talent flowing to Intel.
insights.quote: I hire my good friend Seok-Hee Lee he used to run SK Hynix right so you kind of know something that I'm thinking about

themes.theme: CPU-memory co-design and the DRAM wall

insights.claim: Intel is working not just on new CPU architectures but on embedding CPUs with stacked DRAM, treating vertical CPU-memory integration as the answer to memory bandwidth limits.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: If CPU+stacked-DRAM becomes a product line, packaging and hybrid bonding capacity — not just wafer capacity — becomes the constraint on Intel's server roadmap.
insights.quote: I think CPU and memory I think there's a lot of way we can really do stacking together and also try to find some new architecture from memory
insights.locator: Well you know the you know the first of all

insights.claim: Tan reports that agentic AI and inference workloads are driving huge CPU demand, with much of his day spent on customer calls asking for more CPU supply.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Contradicts the view that AI spend cannibalizes CPU budgets — server CPU units may be a second-order AI beneficiary via inference host demand.
insights.quote: we are very excited you know in the Agentic AI and Inference CPU is huge demand so my day is a lot of CEO call I want to have more CPU from you
insights.locator: Well you know the you know the first of all

insights.claim: Tan argues that a lot of the innovation the memory segment needs simply is not there today, framing the gap itself as the investment opportunity.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: An incumbent CEO calling an adjacent market under-innovated usually precedes either entry or acquisition — screen memory-adjacent IP and startups accordingly.
insights.quote: I think in some way the memory a lot of innovation are not there so there's some really good area.
insights.locator: Well you know the you know the first of all

themes.theme: XBM and ZAM: Intel's DRAM re-entry vehicles

insights.claim: Intel has been quietly working with partners on memory technologies called XBM and ZAM, with ZAM scheduled for 2029-2030 and XBM expected to be unveiled at the start of the next decade.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Puts any Intel memory revenue beyond 2029 — near-term the story is narrative and talent, not P&L.
insights.quote: Intel's ZAM project is scheduled for 2029-2030, while XBM should be unveiled at the start of the next decade.

insights.claim: XBM is framed as Intel course-correcting DRAM ambitions that previously failed with HMC (Hybrid Memory Cube) and MCDRAM, neither of which reached market.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Intel has a documented record of memory programs that never shipped — discount announced timelines accordingly.

insights.claim: Intel's last memory venture, Optane based on 3D XPoint co-developed with Micron, was discontinued in 2022 after losing on cost per dollar to HBM and multi-layer 3D stacked memory.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: The precedent test for any new Intel memory architecture: does it beat HBM on cost per bit, not just on latency or novelty.
insights.quote: competing technologies such as HBM and multi-layer 3D Stacked technologies were showing far better potential and cost/$
insights.locator: Intel's previous venture in the memory space

insights.claim: Intel was founded in 1968 as a memory company, shipping the 3101 SRAM and 1103 DRAM as its first products, making the current move a return rather than a new entry.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Narrative framing management will likely use publicly; useful for anticipating how the story gets sold to investors.
insights.locator: Intel Started As A Memory Business

themes.theme: Structural memory shortage and Intel Foundry leverage

insights.claim: Intel's memory re-entry is timed against heightened shortages across the entire memory segment, with reports cited that shortages persist beyond 2030 as gigawatt-scale AI factories come online.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: A multi-year shortage thesis supports sustained memory pricing — and explains why new entrants think the economics finally work.
insights.quote: Memory shortages will persist beyond 2030, as per the latest reports, as compute and memory demand continues to grow with multiple Gigawatt-scale "AI Factories" coming online

insights.claim: A successful memory return would give Intel Foundry Services logic, memory and leading-edge packaging under one roof, an integration none of its foundry competitors currently offers.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: The bull case for Intel here is a one-stop AI-system foundry pitch; the swing factor is whether customers value integration enough to second-source away from TSMC plus SK Hynix.
insights.locator: If Intel does come back to the memory
